conclusion: The misstatement is wages of AUD 2,010.00 earned from 28 to 30 September 2026 and not accrued at the period end: three of the ten working days of the pay period ending 11 October 2026; it arose in the current period. It is factual: the pay rates and dates come from the payroll register, so there is no doubt about the amount. There is no indication of fraud: the accrual for days worked after the last pay period was omitted.

reasoning_chain.text: Wages and salaries (477) total AUD 33,500.00 for the period.

The payroll register shows three full-time employees who started on 20 July 2026, paid AUD 6,700.00 in total per 14-day pay period in five pay runs from 2 August to 27 September 2026 (AUD 33,500.00 in total); the last pay period ended on 27 September 2026 and the next pay day is 11 October 2026.

A factual misstatement is one about which there is no doubt; a judgemental misstatement arises from management judgements, such as accounting estimates, that the auditor considers unreasonable (ASA 450 para A6).
When the auditor identifies a misstatement, the auditor evaluates whether it is indicative of fraud (ASA 240 para 36).
The wages for days worked before the period end follow from the pay rates and dates in the payroll register, so the misstatement is factual and arose in the current period.
The omission of a routine period-end wages accrual gives no indication of fraud.

counter_argument: A pay run or accrual recorded for 28 to 30 September 2026 would remove the misstatement.
